newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: European internet market seen set to consolidate.
newsitem.headline: European internet market seen set to consolidate.

text.p: Europe's network of internet companies is set to consolidate over the next 18 months, with smaller service providers being swallowed up by telecoms firms and larger providers, an internet conference heard on Monday.
Chris Champion, analyst for the Yankee Group telecoms consultancy, said Europe's internet network had grown up as a patchwork of operations with no single company dominating.

"There is no dominant pan-European player," said Champion, "But I expect a handful of them to emerge over the next 18 months. There aren't any at the moment because it's a nascent market compared to the United States."

Champion told the conference that, unlike in the US, much of the European internet "backbone" infrastructure was still largely in academic and non-profit hands, although commercial firms were involved in building and running those backbones.
He saw cross-border deals emerging as telecoms companies, often with dominating positions in their home markets, looked abroad for more internet business.

"The bigger players, which are the telecoms players and the internet alliances, haven't really moved out of their home markets yet. I expect this to happen very soon," he told Reuters in an interview after his presentation.
Consolidation would happen as the bigger players hunted down the potential revenues on offer, perhaps looking for acquisitions and beefing up alliances.

Champion estimated that the 3.2 million European internet-using households currently generated around $640 million a year in access business. He projected that by 2000 Europe would have 16 million internet households generating over $3.0 billion.

"Europe has woken up late. You could say that 1995 in the US was the year of the internet and internet hype. We really didn't get going until 1996. In a sense we're more subtle and don't fall for the hype and do things at our own speed."
Other reasons for the relatively slow European internet roll-out were comparatively low personal computer ownership rates and high local phone charges, Champion said.

He tipped operators such as UUNet Technologies Inc of the US, Global One, the venture linking Deutsche Telekom, France Telecom and Sprint Corp, and the AT&T Unisource telecoms grouping to emerge as major competitors in the growing European market.
